ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-a2.title: Find the row
ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-a2.body:
Row $k$ has $k$ numbers, so rows $1$ to $9$ contain $45$ numbers and row $10$ starts with the $46$th multiple of $2$, which is $92$. Row $10$ is $92,94,96,98,100,102,\dots,110$. Its digits are $9,2,9,4,9,6,9,8,1,0,0,\dots$, so the $10$th digit is $0$.

**Answer: $0$**

ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-a3.title: Use remainders mod 4
ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-a3.body:
Four consecutive integers $n,n+1,n+2,n+3$ sum to $4n+6$, which leaves remainder $2$ on division by $4$. Squares of positive integers $>1$ are $4,9,16,25,36,\dots$. Check sums of two different squares in increasing order which are of the form $4n+6\ge10$: $4+9=13$, $4+16=20$, $9+16=25$, $4+25=29$, $4+36=40$, $9+25=34$. The sum $34=4\cdot7+6$ is the first of the right form ($7+8+9+10=34$).

**Answer: $34$**

ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-a6.title: Parity and listing
ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-a6.body:
If one of the primes were $2$, its pair would have an odd sum, while every pair of two odd primes has an even sum; the three pairs could not then all have the same sum. So all six primes are odd and the common sum $S$ is even. We need three disjoint pairs of different odd primes with sum $S$:
- $S=10$: $3+7$, $5+5$ (not different) — only one valid pair.
- $S=12,14,16,18$: $12=5+7$; $14=3+11,7+7$; $16=3+13,5+11$; $18=5+13,7+11$ — at most two pairs.
- $S=20$: $3+17,7+13$ — two pairs; $S=22$: $3+19,5+17,11+11$ — two pairs.
- $S=24$: $5+19,7+17,11+13$ — three pairs.

So the least value is $24$.

**Answer: $24$**

ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-a7.title: Bound the integer part
ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-a7.body:
Let $n=\lfloor x\rfloor$. Then $n^2\le nx=260<n(n+1)$, so $n=16$ ($16^2=256\le260<272$). Then $x=260/16=16.25$, and indeed $\lfloor16.25\rfloor=16$.

**Answer: $16.25$**

ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-a8.title: Vertices of the triangle
ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-a8.body:
$y=x$ and $y=-\frac37x$ meet at $(0,0)$. $y=x$ and $y=25-4x$ meet at $(5,5)$. $y=-\frac37x$ and $y=25-4x$ meet where $4x-\frac37x=25$, i.e. $\frac{25}7x=25$, so $x=7$, $y=-3$: the point $(7,-3)$. The area of the triangle with vertices $(0,0),(5,5),(7,-3)$ is $\frac12|5\cdot(-3)-7\cdot5|=\frac12\cdot50=25$.

**Answer: $25$**

ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-a9.title: Use the formulas
ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-a9.body:
The sum of the first $n$ positive integers is $\frac{n(n+1)}2$ and the sum of the first $n$ odd integers is $n^2$. The ratio is $\frac{n+1}{2n}=\frac{23}{44}$, so $44n+44=46n$ and $n=22$.

**Answer: $22$**

ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-a10.title: Coordinates
ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-a10.body:
Put $A=(0,0)$, $B=(1,0)$, $C=(2,0)$, $D=(3,0)$. The semicircle on $AC$ has centre $(1,0)$ and radius $1$; the one on $BD$ has centre $(2,0)$ and radius $1$. Then $Y=(1,1)$ (directly above $B$ on the first semicircle) and $Z=(2,1)$. The semicircles meet at $X=\left(\frac32,\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)$.

The centre of the circle through $Y,Z,X$ lies on the perpendicular bisector $x=\frac32$ of $YZ$; call it $\left(\frac32,k\right)$. Equating distances to $Y$ and $X$: $\frac14+(1-k)^2=\left(k-\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)^2$, so $\frac54-2k=\frac34-\sqrt3k$, giving $k=\frac{1}{2(2-\sqrt3)}=1+\frac{\sqrt3}2$. The radius is $k-\frac{\sqrt3}2=1$.

(Indeed $Y$, $Z$ and $X$ lie at distance $1$ from $\left(\frac32,1+\frac{\sqrt3}2\right)$.)

**Answer: $1$**

ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-a11.title: Compare areas
ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-a11.body:
Let $[ABC]=1$. $AY=\frac{1+3}{10}AB=\frac25AB$, and $AZ=\frac25AC$. Triangle $AYZ$ has area $\frac25\cdot\frac25=\frac4{25}$ (areas scale by the product of the ratios). Triangle $AYC$ has area $\frac25$. So $[ZYC]=[AYC]-[AYZ]=\frac25-\frac4{25}=\frac6{25}$. The ratio is $6:25$.

**Answer: $6:25$**

ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-a12.title: Simplify the fraction
ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-a12.body:
$\frac ac+\frac ab+1=\frac{ab+ac+bc}{bc}$ and $\frac ba+\frac bc+1=\frac{bc+ab+ac}{ac}$ (same numerator). The quotient is $\frac{ac}{bc}=\frac ab$. So $a=17b$.

The inequality becomes $17b+2b+3c\le50$, i.e. $19b+3c\le50$. For $b=1$: $3c\le31$, $c\le10$: $10$ solutions. For $b=2$: $3c\le12$, $c\le4$: $4$ solutions. For $b\ge3$: $19b\ge57>50$. Total $14$ solutions $(a,b,c)$.

**Answer: $14$**

ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-b1.title: Sum of cubes formula
ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-b1.body:
The sum of the first $n$ cubes is $\left(\frac{n(n+1)}2\right)^2$: $1,9,36,100,225,441,784,\dots$ Digit sums: $1,9,9,1,9,9$ — all squares — and then $784\to7+8+4=19$, not a square. So $n=7$.

**Answer: $7$**

ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-b2.title: Find the row
ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-b2.body:
Rows $1$ to $8$ contain $36$ numbers, so row $9$ starts with the $37$th multiple of $2$, $74$, and has $9$ numbers: $74,76,78,80,82,84,86,88,90$. Digit sums: $11,13,15,8,10,12,14,16,9$, total $108$.

**Answer: $108$**

ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-b3.title: Use remainders mod 4
ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-b3.body:
The sum of four consecutive integers is $4n+6\equiv2\pmod4$. Two cubes with an even-remainder-$2$ sum must be both odd (two even cubes give a multiple of $8$, and an odd and an even cube give an odd sum). For an odd $m$, $m^3\equiv m\pmod4$, so for odd bases $a\ne b$ we need $a+b\equiv2\pmod4$. The sums of two different odd cubes (bases $\ge3$) in increasing order start $3^3+5^3=152$ ($3+5\equiv0$, no), $3^3+7^3=370$ ($3+7=10\equiv2$, yes). Any other pair of odd bases has a larger sum ($5^3+7^3=468$, ...). So the smallest is $370=4\cdot91+6$, i.e. $91+92+93+94=370$.

**Answer: $370$**

ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-b4.title: Complement
ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-b4.body:
There are $90000$ five-digit integers. A five-digit palindrome is determined by its first three digits $abc$ with $a\ne0$: $9\cdot10\cdot10=900$. So $90000-900=89100$ are not palindromic.

**Answer: $89100$**

ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-b5.title: Find triangle ABC
ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-b5.body:
The six pieces fit round the centre $O$: $3\times90^\circ+3\theta=360^\circ$, so each isosceles triangle has apex angle $\theta=30^\circ$. Going round, $A$, $B$ and $C$ are the points at the start of each triangle, one every $90^\circ+30^\circ=120^\circ$. They lie on a circle of radius $r$ about $O$ and form an equilateral triangle of side $r\sqrt3$, whose area is $\frac{\sqrt3}4\cdot3r^2=\frac{3\sqrt3}4r^2$. Setting this equal to $12\sqrt3$ gives $r^2=16$ and $r=4$.

**Answer: $4$**

ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-b6.title: Fewest coins, then fix the parity
ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-b6.body:
One of each coin accounts for $388$p, leaving $2019-388=1631$p. The fewest coins for $1631$p are eight £2 coins ($1600$p) and then $31$p $=20+10+1$, which is $3$ more coins: $8+3=11$ coins. So at least $8+11=19$ coins in total. But the number of coins must be even (equal shares), so $19$ is not possible. $20$ is possible: take the $19$-coin collection and replace a $20$p coin by two $10$p coins. Then $20$ coins can be shared $10$ each.

**Answer: $20$**

ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-b7.title: Parity, then try small values
ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-b7.body:
Four different primes with sum $a$: not all can be odd, and if $2$ is among $e,f,g,h$ then $a$ is odd, so $b,c,d$ are odd (no second $2$ is available). Since $a$ is odd it is at least $2+3+5+7=17$; so $a\in\{17,19,23,29,\dots\}$ and $e+f+g+h=2+(x+y+z)$ with $x+y+z=a-2$ for odd primes.

- $a=17$: $x+y+z=15$ forces $\{3,5,7\}$; then $b,c,d$ would be odd primes from $11,13,\dots$ with sum $\ge41$. No.
- $a=19$: three distinct odd primes with sum $17$ do not exist. No.
- $a=23$: $x+y+z=21$ gives $\{3,5,13\}$ or $\{3,7,11\}$; the remaining odd primes below $23$ ($\{7,11,17,19\}$ resp. $\{5,13,17,19\}$) do not contain three with sum $23$. No.
- $a=29$: $29=5+7+17=2+3+11+13$ works.

**Answer: $29$**

ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-b9.title: Similar triangles
ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-b9.body:
Triangles $ZAB$ and $ZYX$ have the angle at $Z$ in common and $\angle ZAB=\angle ZYX$, so they are similar with ratio $\frac{AB}{YX}=\frac5{10}=\frac12$. Let $BZ=t$. Then $ZY=t+4$ and $ZA=\frac12(t+4)$, and $BZ=\frac12 ZX=\frac12(ZA+10)$. So $t=\frac12\left(\frac{t+4}2+10\right)$, giving $4t=t+4+20$ and $t=8$.

**Answer: $8$**

ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-b10.title: Reduce mod 7
ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-b10.body:
$497=7\cdot71$, so $3p$ is divisible by $7$: $p=7p'$. Then $21p'+7q+21r=497$, i.e. $3p'+q+3r=71$. We have $p+q+r=7p'+q+r=7p'+(71-3p'-3r)+r=71+4p'-2r$. To minimise it take $p'=1$ and $r$ as large as possible with $q\ge1$: $3+q+3r=71$ gives $q=68-3r\ge1$, so $r\le22$ and $q=2$. Then $p=7$, $q=2$, $r=22$: $7+2+22=31$ (check: $21+14+462=497$).

**Answer: $31$**

ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-b12.title: Eliminate y
ukmt-stmc-2018-19-final-relay-b12.body:
From the first equation $y=-kx^2-10$. Substituting into the second: $k^2x^2-2kx^2-20-12=0$, so $x^2k(k-2)=32$. As $x$ is an integer, $x^2\in\{1,4,16\}$ ($x^2\mid32$, $x\ne0$ since $x=0$ gives $y=-10$ and $y=6$): so $k(k-2)\in\{32,8,2\}$. $k^2-2k-32=0$ and $k^2-2k-2=0$ have no integer roots. $k^2-2k-8=0$ gives $k=4$ or $k=-2$ (with $x=\pm2$).

Check: $k=4$, $x=2$: $y=-26$; second equation: $16\cdot4-52-12=0$ ✓. $k=-2$, $x=2$: $y=-2$; second: $4\cdot4-4-12=0$ ✓.

**Answer: $k=-2$ and $k=4$**
